title: Cisco Secure Workload Alert Volume
exclusions: Counts syslog alerts from Secure Workload. It does not parse policy or workload names, which the add-on does not publish as fields.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Generate a test alert in Secure Workload and confirm the next hour's alerts count increases after the syslog connector delivers it.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Disable the syslog connector. The following hour is zero while the console still shows alerts.

dataSources: `index=cisco_secure_workload sourcetype=cisco:secure:workload` from the Cisco Security Cloud (7404) Secure Workload input, which listens for syslog. A syslog connector is configured on the Secure Workload side to that port. The user guide publishes no field list, so the search counts events.
app: Cisco Security Cloud (`CiscoSecurityCloud`, [Splunkbase 7404](https://splunkbase.splunk.com/app/7404)), Secure Workload input.

description: Counts Cisco Secure Workload alerts per hour. The add-on receives them as syslog with sourcetype cisco:secure:workload and publishes no field names, so the search counts alerts instead of grouping by workload.
value: A policy violation on a server is only visible next to the rest of the incident if the syslog connector is delivering. This count is the check that microsegmentation alerts are still arriving.
implementation: Create the Secure Workload input in Cisco Security Cloud and point the Secure Workload syslog connector at its port. Chart alerts per hour.
visualization: Column chart of alerts per hour over 24 hours.

references.title: Cisco Security Cloud App for Splunk User Guide

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Policy tests** — a change window that hits many workloads produces a spike. Note the window before treating it as an attack.

**Suppression:** alert when a staffed hour is zero.
detailedImplementation:
Prerequisites
• Cisco Security Cloud (`CiscoSecurityCloud`, Splunkbase 7404) on the search heads and on the heavy forwarder or Splunk Cloud Inputs Data Manager that runs its modular inputs.
• A syslog connector on Secure Workload aimed at the input's address and port.
• An index for this data (this page uses `cisco_secure_workload`) and a role with `srchIndexesAllowed` on it for the SOC.

Step 1 — Configure data collection
• In Cisco Security Cloud open Application Setup, choose the Secure Workload card, and create an input. Set the index to `cisco_secure_workload`.
• The input writes `cisco:secure:workload`.
• Confirm events arrive: `index=cisco_secure_workload sourcetype="cisco:secure:workload" | stats count`.

Step 2 — Create the search
```spl
index=cisco_secure_workload sourcetype="cisco:secure:workload" earliest=-24h
| timechart span=1h count as alerts
```

Understanding this SPL
• The user guide describes a syslog listener, not an API poll. The connector on the Secure Workload side must target the input's address and port.
• No workload or policy field is documented, so the panel counts events.

Step 3 — Validate
• In Secure Workload, open the alerts for the same hour. A console with alerts and a zero panel means syslog is not arriving.

• Confirm in the vendor console that the same hour shows the same kind of event before trusting a zero or a spike.

Step 4 — Operationalize
• Put the panel on the SOC dashboard for Secure Workload and refresh it hourly.
• Alert when the count drops to zero during a staffed period, which means the input stopped, and throttle for 4 hours.

Step 5 — Troubleshooting
• Nothing arrives: the connector points at the wrong port, or a firewall blocks UDP or TCP syslog from the Secure Workload appliance to the input host.
• Events arrive under a different sourcetype: the input's sourcetype was edited. The default the add-on ships is cisco:secure:workload.
• No data for this sourcetype, with an input error in the Cisco Security Cloud log, means the credential or token is incorrect.
grandmaExplanation: We count the workload alerts Cisco sends each hour, so we know server policy violations are still reaching us.
